LAREDO — Mayor Dr. Victor D. Treviño is asking voters to keep him in office on November 3. His campaign's 30th-day-before-election finance report — covering July 1 through September 24, 2026, according to the City Secretary's posting — was filed with the City Secretary and posted on the City of Laredo's campaign finance reports page under the October 5, 2026 deadline. It is an 11-page public record, and it answers a question every voter is entitled to ask of an incumbent: who is paying for this campaign?

The headline numbers

For the July 1 – September 24 period, the report lists total political contributions of $2,000 and total political expenditures of $17,736.15, with $200,000 in outstanding loans and $2,000 in contributions maintained — the cash left on hand at the end of the period. The rest of the support behind the mayor's campaign did not arrive as cash at all: the report also lists $32,122.16 in in-kind contributions, and that $200,000 in loans came from the mayor himself. His July 15, 2026 semiannual report, covering the first half of the year, is also on file with the City Secretary. One more report — the 8th-day-before-election filing, covering September 25 through October 24 — is due October 26 and had not been posted as of October 23.

The names on the filing

The contributions itemized in the report fit on a very short page. Schedule A1 lists exactly one cash donor: Lucas Galvan of Laredo, identified in the filing as a business owner, who gave $2,000 on August 17, 2026. The campaign's visible muscle came in kind instead. On Schedule A2, the Laredo Fire PAC contributed $29,122.16 worth of billboards and sign installation, dated September 21, 2026, and Cheetah Rentals, LLC contributed $3,000 worth of political advertising, dated September 17, 2026. As printed in the filing, Cheetah Rentals' address is 101 West Village Blvd, Suite B — the same building as the Suite A address the mayor lists elsewhere in the same report. Webb Watch notes the shared address as a fact of the document and draws no conclusion from it. None of this is illegal — Texas sets no contribution limits in local races, and every dollar was disclosed, as the law requires. But disclosure exists so voters can judge for themselves whose support a candidate carries into office.

His own money — a $200,000 loan from the mayor to the mayor

The largest single source of money in the report is Treviño himself. Schedule E shows a $200,000 loan made on June 30, 2026 — the day before this reporting period opened — by Dr. Victor D. Trevino, at 101 West Village Blvd, Suite A. The lender is not a bank: the form lists the lender's occupation as Mayor and his employer as the City of Laredo, with no collateral. The loan carries interest of 7.00 percent, and it does not come due until December 12, 2029. If voters give Treviño the second term he is asking for, that loan stays on his campaign's books deep into the new term — and until it is repaid, his campaign owes the mayor personally, principal plus 7 percent interest (at that rate, interest on the full $200,000 runs $14,000 a year). The report also shows the mayor spending from his own pocket along the way: $7,480 in personal-funds expenditures on Schedule G — paid mostly to local media and advertising vendors — and $10,256.15 charged on a CitiBank credit card on Schedule F4. Together, those two schedules account for every dollar of the $17,736.15 the campaign reported spending.

Why it matters for an incumbent

A challenger's donor list shows who wants a change. An incumbent's shows something else: who has done well under the current administration and wants it to continue — and who has business pending before the mayor and council right now. In Treviño's case, the striking fact is how short the list is: one $2,000 check, the firefighters' PAC's billboards, a rental company's advertising, and a six-figure loan from the candidate. Treviño, a physician and former health authority, is running on water infrastructure, public safety, and healthcare. The names financing that message are printed in his own report, in black and white, for anyone to read.

The rest of the field, for scale

In the same reporting period, Council Member Alyssa Cigarroa reported $374,500 in contributions — the money leader of the race by far. JD Gonzalez reported no contributions at all, financing his campaign entirely with loans from himself. Poncho Casso reported $4,000 from two donors. And Jorge A. Garza, the fifth name on the mayoral ballot, filed no 30th-day report. Against that field, Treviño's $2,000 in cash contributions is the smallest amount of outside money raised by any candidate who filed — his campaign runs on his own credit instead.

The bottom line

A campaign finance report is not an accusation. It is a list of names and numbers that the law makes public precisely so voters can weigh them. Treviño's filing shows a reelection campaign carried almost entirely by the incumbent himself — one donor, one PAC's billboards, and a $200,000 loan at 7 percent interest that his campaign will still owe him if he wins. Whether that is the independence of a man beholden to no one, or a one-man operation with a one-man donor list, is a judgment the report leaves, properly, to the voters of Laredo.

title: Follow the Money: Who Is Financing Mayor Victor Treviño's Reelection?
